sentences.text: Revenue (net interest income plus noninterest income) grew from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was not smooth: revenue rose 15.8% in FY2023 to $28.0 billion, fell 2.4% in FY2024 to $27.3 billion, then recovered 4.4% in FY2025 [D189][D169][D214][D194][D239][D219].
The FY2023 step change came from an 18.1% rise in net interest income, driven by higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition [D184][P33].
The FY2024 dip reflected a 6.4% fall in net interest income from higher rates on deposit mix and pricing [D209][P21].
Payment Services was the steadiest contributor, adding 1.4pp to revenue growth in FY2025 on 5.4% segment growth and a 25.8% revenue share [D261][D260][D259].
That segment's net revenue rose 5.4% on higher average loan balances, lower funding costs and higher merchant processing and card revenue from sales volume [P4].
Consumer and Business Banking shrank, subtracting 1.3pp in FY2025 as segment revenue fell 3.9% and its share slipped to 31.0% [D253][D252][D251].
Its net revenue fell on deposit mix changes and second-quarter loan sales, partly offset by higher mortgage banking revenue [P6].
Net income grew 20.2% in FY2025 against 4.4% revenue growth, so costs fell faster than revenue [D227][D239].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025, below its 59.3% window median and well inside the 55.3% low and 67.4% high [D220][D277][D275][D276].
That is 2.7pp better than the 61.7% banks peer median and sits in the 14th percentile of seven peers [D220][D281][D280].
Noninterest expense fell 2.0% in FY2025 on prior-year merger and integration charges, lower compensation and the prior-year FDIC special assessment [D238][P10].
The FY2023 efficiency spike to 67.4% came from a 26.6% expense increase driven by MUB merger charges and a $734 million FDIC special assessment [D170][D188][P30].
The effective tax rate held near 20.2% in FY2025, so net margin of 26.5% tracked the operating result rather than a below-the-line swing [D215][D223].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return is the better test [F60][F30].
Operating cash flow of $7.97 billion was 1.05x net income in FY2025, in line with the 1.04x of FY2017 but below the 1.80x of FY2024 [F60][F30][D216][D13][D191].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.66 billion equaled 48% of FY2025 net income, up from $3.27 billion in FY2024 [D218][F30][D193].
Return on average equity rose to 12.2% in FY2025 from 11.1% in FY2024, above the 11.8% banks peer median and in the 71st percentile of seven peers [D226][D201][D283][D282].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits, down from 80.5% in FY2016, leaving more liquidity on the balance sheet [D224][D10].
The allowance was 2.0% of loans, up from 1.5% in FY2019, and the credit-loss provision was 7.7% of revenue against a 6.1% peer median [D225][D72][D221][D285].
Buybacks fell to $489 million in FY2025 from $4.53 billion in FY2019, while dividends rose to $3.17 billion, and the diluted share count was flat at 1,558 million [X85][X79][X95][X75][D237].
Revenue declined 2.4% in FY2024 to $27.3 billion, the one flagged period, driven by the 6.4% net interest income fall [R1][D214][D194][D209].
The cause was higher rates pressuring deposit mix and pricing, and the FY2025 recovery to $28.5 billion shows it was cyclical rather than structural [P21][D219].
The provision ran 7.7% of revenue in FY2025 against a 6.1% peer median, a persistent gap worth monitoring [D221][D285].
If the efficiency ratio moves back above the 59.3% window median, the cost discipline behind the FY2025 earnings growth would be reversing [D277][D220].
If net interest income growth falls back below the FY2025 2.2% rate, the loan-growth and funding-cost tailwind described in the FY2025 10-K would be fading [D234][P15].
If the credit-loss provision rises above the 7.7% of revenue recorded in FY2025, the stabilizing-credit narrative would be under pressure [D221][P12].
